periods.activity_title: Reading the Informational Text Aloud and Together

time_bands.activity: Teacher invites students to name any large water container they have seen near their home or school. A quick show of hands reveals who has seen an overhead tank — this warm curiosity opens the text without revealing its content.

Teacher reads the full text of 'What a Tank!' aloud (Textbook pp.65–78), pausing after each new water structure — Ooranis, Panam Keni, Tanka, overhead tanks — to point to any accompanying illustration and let the name settle.

Shared reading: students join the teacher for a second read of the section on Punjab's sculpted tanks (the passage beginning with the description of flower, football, and rooster shapes), reading aloud together in a steady voice.

Brief whole-class pause: teacher asks, 'Which water structure surprised you most?' Two or three students share one word or one sentence — no extended discussion yet, just first impressions recorded on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: This first encounter with the text is about building familiarity with its range — from ancient Ooranis and Panam Keni wells to the sculpted tanks of rural Punjab — before any task is set. Pronunciation of 'Oorani', 'Panam Keni', and 'Tanka' may need a slow modelled read; invite students to repeat each name once. Keep listening and reading unhurried here.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think (p.68): answer questions on water tanks and Punjab's sculpted designs.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes the four discussion questions from 'Let us Think' on the board. Students read them silently for a moment, then turn to their neighbour to share one quick thought — this activates the text they encountered through the read-aloud.

Let us Think (p.68): teacher leads Q1 ('What do we use a water tank for?') and Q2 ('Where is Punjab located on the map of India?') as a whole-class discussion, inviting multiple answers and pointing to a map of India if one is available.

Let us Think (p.68): teacher leads Q3 ('How are the water tanks in Punjab made?') and Q4 ('How do the unique shapes reflect the identity of the owner?'). Students are asked to find evidence in the text before answering, building the habit of text-referencing.

Students write one-sentence answers to all four questions in their notebooks. Teacher circulates and offers brief oral feedback on completeness, especially checking that Q4 responses mention a specific shape and its connection to occupation or passion.

periods.teacher_notes: The prose summary notes that Punjab's tank shapes — flowers, footballs, roosters, tractors, aeroplanes — each reflect the owner's identity or occupation; students who give only a list of shapes without the identity link should be prompted with 'Why that shape for that family?' For Q2, a physical or digital map of India placed at the front helps students locate Punjab in the north-west before answering. Students who have read the text in the earlier read-aloud will have a clear advantage here — encourage quieter students to locate the answer in the book rather than waiting for classmates to supply it.

periods.activity_title: Speaking About Water — Let us Think and Let us Speak

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think (p.68): oral discussion on other ways to store water and imagined tank design.
Let us Speak (p.68): group discussion on water wastage with written examples and class sharing.

time_bands.activity: Let us Think B (p.68): teacher poses Q1 ('Do you know any other ways of storing water?') to the class. Students call out responses — buckets, pots, ponds, rivers, rainwater harvesting — while the teacher lists them on the board, briefly connecting each to the structures described in the text.

Let us Think B (p.68): teacher poses Q2 ('If you had to build a water tank, what would it look like? Why?'). Students think for a moment, then share with a partner before two or three pairs present their idea to the class, giving a shape and a reason.

Let us Speak A+B (p.68): students form groups of three. Each group discusses how water is wasted daily and what can be done, then writes at least three examples in their notebooks in the format 'Wastage — Solution'. Teacher circulates, prompting groups who are stuck with the printed example about running water while brushing teeth.

Each group shares one example with the class. Teacher notes the most original observations on the board. The board list of examples serves as the group's shared reference for the conversation and is not taken away — the writing stays in each student's notebook.

periods.teacher_notes: Students tend to name only taps and bottles as water storage — guiding them toward the text's traditional structures (Ooranis, Panam Keni, Tanka) enriches this conversation with content from the informational text. For the tank-design question, accept playful or personal answers without evaluation; the point is connecting identity to design, exactly as the text does for Punjab's tank owners. Groups that finish their three examples quickly can be asked to add a fourth from outside the home, such as a school or park.

periods.activity_title: Listening to 'A Day without Water' and Responding

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Listen (pp.74–75): listen to passage and answer five comprehension questions.

homework.task_brief: Let us Speak C (p.68): say aloud the phrase pairs 'What a tank!'/'Water tank' and 'I scream'/'Ice cream'; note answers to the Yes/No questions in notebook.

time_bands.activity: Teacher tells students they will hear a short story about a girl named Suma who wakes up one morning to no water. Students are asked to listen carefully and remember what happens to Suma at school — this listening focus helps them track the narrative arc.

Let us Listen (pp.74–75): teacher reads the full passage 'A Day without Water' aloud at a measured pace, then reads it a second time while students listen again. After the second reading, teacher pauses and asks the class to say aloud one thing they remember — no books, no notes yet.

Teacher reads the passage a third time. Students may now follow along if they wish. After the third reading, the five comprehension questions are read aloud one by one, and students note their chosen option in their notebooks.

Let us Listen (pp.74–75): teacher goes through each of the five questions, calling on different students for answers and confirming the correct option with a brief reference to the passage — for example, confirming that Suma and her neighbours 'bought bottles and waited for tankers' by re-reading that sentence aloud.

Quick oral close: teacher asks, 'What did Suma's school call the event they organised?' Students respond chorally. This last beat reinforces the Water Conservation Week detail before the sitting ends.

periods.teacher_notes: The passage 'A Day without Water' is read by the teacher from Textbook pp.74–75 — three full readings align with NCF's guidance for preparatory listening tasks. Students who ask to look at the text during the first two readings should be gently redirected to listening; the third read allows them to follow along. The five questions test recall rather than inference, so students who listened carefully should answer confidently; for those who hesitate, teacher re-reads the relevant sentence rather than giving the answer directly.

periods.activity_title: Contractions — Let us Learn A and B

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn A (p.69): write contractions for six 'not' word pairs.
Let us Learn B (p.69): rewrite two paragraphs using contracted forms of underlined words.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes 'are not → aren't' and 'would not → wouldn't' on the board and explains contractions: two words joined, some letters removed, an apostrophe marks the gap. Students are asked to find one contraction in the listening passage they heard earlier ('couldn't', 'didn't') to show contractions in real text.

Let us Learn A (p.69): students work individually, writing contractions for the six word pairs (do not, is not, are not, cannot, could not, did not) in their notebooks. Teacher circulates and notes common errors — particularly 'can't' (one fewer letter than expected) — for whole-class correction.

Quick whole-class check: teacher calls out each word pair, a student writes the contraction on the board, and the class reads it aloud together. Any error is corrected immediately with an explanation of which letters the apostrophe replaces.

Let us Learn B (p.69): teacher reads paragraph 1 (Partho) aloud, students identify underlined words, then rewrite the paragraph in their notebooks using contractions. Teacher checks a few books before moving to paragraph 2 (Tina), which students complete independently.

periods.teacher_notes: The most frequent error at this stage is placing the apostrophe after the second word rather than in place of the omitted letters — modelling 'do not → don't' by physically crossing out the 'o' and inserting the apostrophe on the board is effective. 'Cannot → can't' is irregular in that two letters are lost, not one; flag this explicitly. Tasks C, D, E, and F from Let us Learn are not anchored in this unit; students who wish to explore exclamatory sentences and animal family names may do so independently using Textbook pp.69–72.

periods.activity_title: Exclamatory Sentences and Animal Families — Let us Learn C and E

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn C (p.69–70): read exclamatory sentences, identify them, name four emotions.
Let us Learn E (p.71): read animal family labels from pictures; say and sort them.

homework.task_brief: Let us Learn D (p.70): find five exclamatory sentences from Grade 4 textbook and record each with its emotion in a table.

time_bands.activity: Let us Learn C (pp.69–70): teacher reads the three example exclamatory sentences aloud with strong expression, then asks students why each one ends with an exclamation mark. Class identifies the emotion in each ('creative' = admiration, 'rooster, tractor, football' = surprise, 'Hurrah!' = joy) and brainstorms four emotions together — teacher writes them on the board.

Quick practice: teacher calls out an everyday situation ('Your team wins a game!') and students compose one exclamatory sentence aloud. Two or three students share; the class decides whether the sentence needs an exclamation mark and identifies the emotion.

Let us Learn E (p.71): teacher holds the book open to the animal family pictures and reads each label aloud (lion–lioness–lion cub; tiger–tigress–tiger cub; rooster–hen–chick; bull–cow–calf; stallion–mare–foal). Students repeat chorally after each family. Then teacher calls out one member (e.g. 'tigress') and students respond with the full family name.

Pair game: one student in each pair says a family member's name, the partner says the other two. Teacher circulates listening for accuracy with the less familiar families (stallion–mare–foal). The game ends with a whole-class chant of all five families in sequence.

periods.teacher_notes: The exclamatory sentence from the chapter — 'He saw a rooster, a tractor, and a giant football, all made of cement!' — is a useful anchor here because students have already read it in the text; connecting grammar to that familiar sentence makes the rule memorable. The animal family vocabulary (stallion, mare, foal; rooster, hen, chick) is new at Grade V and benefits from repeated oral production — the pair game and final chant give two more exposures after the teacher-led reading. Task D (finding exclamatory sentences in the Grade 4 textbook) is set as homework; students should write the table in their notebooks.

periods.activity_title: Designing a Water Tank Awareness Poster — Let us Write A

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write A (p.73): design and write a poster for a community water-tank awareness campaign.

homework.task_brief: Let us Write B (p.73): write ten words ending in '-er', ten in '-or', and ten in '-at' in notebook.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes the poster topic ('Save Our Water Tanks — A Community Awareness Campaign') on the board and shows students how a poster is structured: a bold headline, a slogan in fewer than eight words, bullet points, and a practical call to action with a time and place. This modelled frame stays on the board throughout the unit.

Shared planning: class brainstorms slogans aloud — teacher accepts three or four, writes them on the board, and the class picks the most persuasive. Students then suggest two bullet points on why water tanks matter, drawing on facts from the text (flooding prevention, year-round storage, community use).

Let us Write A (p.73): students design and write their own poster in the space provided in the textbook (or in their notebooks). Teacher circulates, checking that each poster has all four required components — topic heading, slogan, bullet points, and an invitation with time and place — and offers brief oral prompts to students who are stuck on the call-to-action section.

Two or three students hold up their posters and read their slogans aloud. The class gives a thumbs-up for the slogan they find most memorable. Teacher notes one strong model and one area for the class to improve (e.g. adding a specific time/date to the cleaning-drive invitation).

periods.teacher_notes: Many students will write a strong slogan but forget the practical invitation (place and time of the cleaning drive); prompting with 'Who should come, where, and when?' is usually enough to unlock that section. The modelled frame on the board prevents blank-page anxiety — students may copy the structure but must generate their own slogan and bullet points. Task B (words ending in '-er', '-or', '-at') is set as homework to keep this unit focused on extended writing.

periods.activity_title: The Thirsty Crow Visits Our School — Let us Explore B

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Explore B (p.78): enact the school's invitation to the Thirsty Crow using the picture series.

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens the textbook to the four sequential pictures of the Thirsty Crow (p.78) and walks students through them one by one, eliciting what the crow does in each picture. Students briefly retell the story in two or three sentences to check shared familiarity before the enactment begins.

Teacher sets the imaginative frame: 'Our school has invited the clever crow to speak to us about its famous water-problem solution.' Roles are assigned — one student as the crow, three or four as student interviewers, the rest as the school audience. The teacher models one interviewer question ('Crow, how did you know the stones would raise the water?') to show the register students should use.

Let us Explore B (p.78): the enactment runs with teacher guiding from the side. The crow explains its problem and solution; interviewers ask at least two questions each; the audience may call out one question at the end. Teacher pauses briefly between the crow's answers to prompt the next interviewer rather than letting the performance stall.

Whole-class reflection: teacher asks students to connect the crow's ingenuity to the chapter's theme — both the crow and the water-tank builders of Punjab found creative solutions to a water-related challenge. Two or three students share the connection in one sentence each, closing the chapter's ideas on a celebratory note.

periods.teacher_notes: The Thirsty Crow story is described as already familiar to students in the text; the teacher's role is to keep the enactment moving rather than re-teaching the story. If a student playing the crow hesitates, offer a sentence starter such as 'I was very thirsty and I saw a pot of water, but…'. The closing reflection — linking the crow's stone-dropping ingenuity to Punjab's sculpted tanks as expressions of creative problem-solving around water — brings the chapter's informational and imaginative strands together. Task A (researching tank-cleaning techniques and making a chart) is an extended project best suited to students who wish to continue independently; flag it as a self-study extension using Textbook p.77.

items.source_context: Water storage structures — Ooranis, Panam Keni, Tanka, Punjab's sculpted overhead tanks — and their cultural significance.
items.item_stem:
Read the three statements below. Write True or False for each one.
1. Tankas in Rajasthan are underground water stores that can hold water for six to seven months.
2. Panam Keni wells are found in Tamil Nadu and dry up every summer.
3. The overhead tanks of rural Punjab are made in decorative shapes such as flowers, roosters, and aeroplanes.

options.text: Panam Keni wells are found in Tamil Nadu and dry up every summer.
Tankas in Rajasthan are underground water stores that can hold water for six to seven months.
The overhead tanks of rural Punjab are made in decorative shapes such as flowers, roosters, and aeroplanes.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1 — True: the text explicitly states Tankas store water for six to seven months. 2 — False: Panam Keni wells are in Kerala and stay full year-round; Ooranis are in Tamil Nadu. 3 — True: the text names flowers, footballs, roosters, tractors, and aeroplanes as shapes used in Punjab.

Gives a plausible reason using the text's idea.

Your teacher will read the passage 'A Day without Water' aloud. Listen carefully, then choose the correct answer.
When Suma went to school on the day there was no water, what were the students told to bring from home?

what_each_option_reveals.B: Suggests the student may have confused the school announcement with a general daily-routine detail.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Indicates the student associated the hot summer morning with weather-related items rather than the water shortage.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Suggests the student recalled the school setting but did not connect the shortage to a specific shortage-response item.

expected_elements: Describes a specific situation without water.
Mentions one way people managed or coped.
Suggests or describes at least one solution.

Fill in each blank with the correct contraction of the words in brackets.
1. She ________ (did not) know the tank was shaped like a rooster.
2. The workers ________ (could not) finish the cement frame in one day.
3. We ________ (are not) allowed to waste water.
4. He ________ (is not) sure which village has the biggest tank.

expected_elements: Says a complete sentence ending with an exclamation.
Names the emotion the sentence expresses.

items.item_stem: Match each description of what the Thirsty Crow did with the correct step in its problem-solving journey.

What the crow did | Step in the journey
Found a pot with a little water at the bottom | Recognised the problem
Dropped stones into the pot one by one | Tried a creative solution
Watched the water level rise slowly | Saw the solution working
Drank the water when it reached the top | Solved the problem successfully

items.item_stem: The Thirsty Crow solved a water problem using stones and creativity. The tank builders of Punjab solved a water-storage problem by sculpting tanks into beautiful shapes. Speak for about a minute: In what way are the crow and the Punjab tank builders similar? Use one detail from each to support your answer.

Names one creative feature of Punjab's tanks.
